CVE-2024-36127.title: apko is an apk-based OCI image builder. apko exposures HTTP basic ...
CVE-2024-36127.description: apko is an apk-based OCI image builder. apko exposures HTTP basic auth credentials from repository and keyring URLs in log output. This vulnerability is fixed in v0.14.5.

CVE-2026-105768.title: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built ...
CVE-2026-105768.description: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built from apk packages. From version 0.2.0 to before version 1.4.5, UserEntry.Parse and GroupEntry.Parse in pkg/passwd read the UID and GID fields of /etc/passwd and /etc/group entries with strconv.Atoi and convert them to uint32 without a range check. On 64-bit platforms an out-of-range value such as 4294967296 (2^32) is truncated to 0, and negative values wrap. Because apko parses the passwd and group entries supplied by the packages it installs and writes them back into the image, an attacker who controls a package installed into the image can ship an entry that appears to declare an unprivileged UID or GID but is written into the built image as UID 0 or GID 0 (root). The truncated UID is also used when resolving the image's run-as user. This issue has been fixed in version 1.4.5.

CVE-2026-42575.title: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built ...
CVE-2026-42575.description: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built from apk packages. Prior to version 1.2.7, apko verifies the signature on APKINDEX.tar.gz but never compares individually downloaded .apk packages against the checksum recorded in the signed index. The checksum is parsed and available via ChecksumString(), and the downloaded package control hash is computed, but the two values are never compared in getPackageImpl(). Mismatched packages are silently accepted. An attacker who can substitute download responses (compromised mirror, HTTP repository, poisoned CDN cache) can install arbitrary packages into built images. This issue has been patched in version 1.2.7.

CVE-2026-42576.title: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built ...
CVE-2026-42576.description: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built from apk packages. Prior to version 1.2.7, DiscoverKeys in pkg/apk/apk/implementation.go unconditionally type-asserts JWKS keys as *rsa.PublicKey without checking the key type. If a repository JWKS endpoint returns a non-RSA key (e.g. EC), the unchecked assertion panics and crashes apko. This affects any workflow that initializes the APK database and fetches repository keys. This issue has been patched in version 1.2.7.

GHSA-389p-892w-qwgf.title: Control characters in package data allow forging apk installed-database records
GHSA-389p-892w-qwgf.description: ### Impact apko writes the apk installed database (`/lib/apk/db/installed`) as a newline-delimited `<token>:<value>` record format, rendering attacker-influenced data into those lines verbatim with no escaping or validation. A crafted package can embed a newline in that data, terminating the current record and forging an entire additional package record. The installed database is the source for SBOM generation (`pkg/build/sbom.go`, `pkg/build/build.go`), so forged records propagate into apko's SPDX output. The significant consequence is **concealment** rather than addition: an attacker who can place a package in a repository the build trusts can install a vulnerable component while forging a record that reports a different name or version, causing downstream vulnerability scanners that consume the SBOM to miss the real component. ### Scope This advisory covers one mechanism: **control characters — a newline in particular — carried in package data into installed-database records.** It does not claim to close every route by which a package can misrepresent itself in the SBOM. The fix is the byte-level validation described under Patches, not a general guarantee that recorded package identity matches the package installed. ### Affected data paths Three distinct families of attacker-influenced data reach these records. All were unvalidated. **1. Package metadata from `.PKGINFO` (no filesystem interaction required).** `PackageToInstalled` (`pkg/apk/apk/package.go`) renders `P:`, `V:`, `T:`, `L:`, `o:`, `m:`, `U:`, `D:`, `p:`, `r:` and `c:` lines directly from parsed `.PKGINFO` values. apk-tools reads `.PKGINFO` as a plain `key = value` line splitter with no quoting, and so can neither produce nor observe a multi-line value. apko parses it with `gopkg.in/ini.v1` (`pkg/apk/types/package.go`), which honours backquoted and triple-quoted multi-line values by default. A triple-quoted `pkgdesc` therefore carries an embedded newline straight into the database. This is the most accessible variant — it needs nothing more than a crafted `pkgdesc` field, and apko explicitly prefers `.PKGINFO` over APKINDEX as the more complete source (`pkg/apk/apk/implementation.go`), so the permissive parser is the one that reaches the database. **2. Archive entry names.** `AddInstalledPackage` (`pkg/apk/apk/installed.go`) writes `F:` and `R:` lines from `tar.Header.Name`. No control-character validation existed anywhere in `pkg/apk`; `sanitizeArchivePath` guards only path traversal. Both install paths were affected — `installAPKFiles` and the `lazilyInstallAPKFiles` fastpath that `installPackage` selects whenever the backing filesystem implements `WriteHeaderer`, which is the normal apko configuration. Control-section entry names reached `usr/lib/apk/db/scripts.tar` in the produced image by the same route, via `updateScriptsTar`. **3. PAX checksum records.** The `Z:` line forwards an `APK-TOOLS.checksum.SHA1` PAX record unchanged when it already carries a `Q1` prefix. `installAPKFiles` recomputes that record for regular files, but the symlink and hardlink branches pass the supplied value through untouched. Additionally, an empty archive entry name reached an unguarded `header.Name[0]` index and panicked both install paths (`runtime error: index out of range [0] with length 0`). `archive/tar` encodes an empty `Name` without complaint, so a malicious package crashed apko outright — a denial of service in a library consumed by melange. ### Affected versions All released versions through v1.2.39. Confirmed reproducible end to end: a single `AddInstalledPackage` call yielding two packages from `GetInstalled`, both via a crafted `.PKGINFO` and via a crafted entry name. ### Attack prerequisites The attacker must be able to introduce a package into a repository that the build trusts, or otherwise control the contents of an installed package. This is a meaningful precondition and is the primary reason for the moderate severity rating rather than a higher one. No filesystem-level access or unusual configuration is required. ### Patches Fixed by validating at each source and again at the sink: - `.PKGINFO` values containing a newline or carriage return are rejected at parse time in `types.ParsePackageInfo`, restoring agreement with apk-tools about what the format permits with respect to line breaks. The check is reflective over the struct, and a field whose type it cannot walk is a hard error rather than a silent skip, so a field added later cannot escape validation unnoticed. - Archive entry names containing a byte below `0x20` or equal to `0x7f`, or that are empty, are rejected on both install paths and in `updateScriptsTar`, via a typed `InvalidEntryNameError`. This mirrors apk-tools byte for byte. - `AddInstalledPackage` also receives names read back out of an existing image's database, which apko re-writes when building on that image as a base. Applying the strict class there would fail builds over bytes already present in a third-party base image, and silently dropping the entry would conceal a file that is really present, so that sink rejects only the bytes that break the record format — newline and carriage return. Neither can reach it from a database read. An empty name is accepted there because it is the representation of the top-level directory. - Every rendered database line is checked for an embedded newline or carriage return immediately before the record is written, which covers the `Z:` passthrough and any field that acquires such a value in future. The record is now built entirely before the database file is opened, so a rejection cannot leave a created-but-empty database behind. - `ParseInstalled` no longer returns a short package list with a nil error when a record line exceeds the scanner's buffer. An over-long line previously stopped the scan silently, so a single such line erased every record after it from the parsed result and therefore from the SBOM — the same concealment impact, reached without a control character. The bound is raised to accommodate legitimately long dependency lines, and exceeding it is now an error. - `ParseInstalled` no longer discards `sanitizeArchivePath`'s error, which had converted a path traversal in an `R:` value into a file header with an empty name. - An install that fails part-way leaves entries written and claimed in the in-memory ownership map, which later packages' records are filtered against. Those writes cannot be safely unwound, so the affected `APK` value now refuses further installs and record writes with `ErrInstallAborted` rather than producing records built from a stale view. ### Upstream context apk-tools addressed the entry-name half of this class in commit [`c1594f60`](https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/apk-tools/-/commit/c1594f60770483625891541375a074fe07338401) (2021-02-04), 'db: consider control characters in filename as malicious', reported by Luca Weiss, with the rationale that 'especially a newline can produce havoc in the database file as the filename is written there as-is'. It added a `contains_control_character()` check rejecting any byte below `0x20` or equal to `0x7f`. It shipped in apk-tools v2.12.2 and, as far as we can determine, was never assigned a CVE. apko reimplements apk in Go and did not inherit this hardening. The initial upstream implementation used a signed `char` comparison, which incorrectly rejected all non-ASCII (multi-byte UTF-8) names; corrected three days later in [`ab7b8e3`](https://gitlab.alpinelinux.org/alpine/apk-tools/-/commit/ab7b8e3c995eb5a05ddbaa4546cd16a10da2d836) ('db: fix control character check to use uint8_t', alpine issue #10737). The Go port compares unsigned bytes and carries regression tests pinning that legitimate UTF-8 names remain acceptable. Upstream applies `contains_control_character()` to the archive entry name only — `src/database.c`, one call site, on `ae->name`. apko matches that scope deliberately: link targets are not validated, because they never become an `F:` or `R:` value and so cannot forge a record, and rejecting them would refuse packages that `apk add` installs without complaint. The metadata variant has no upstream analogue, because apk-tools' line-based `.PKGINFO` reader cannot represent it. ### Related Before [#2328](https://github.com/chainguard-dev/apko/pull/2328), an entry name embedding a single-character line also reached an out-of-range slice panic in `ParseInstalled`, making that denial of service reachable from a package rather than only from a corrupt base image. That specific path is closed by #2328. Two adjacent defects found during this work were fixed publicly ahead of this advisory, as neither was reachable from a package: an infinite loop walking to the filesystem root ([#2389](https://github.com/chainguard-dev/apko/pull/2389)) and a silently discarded record for a package with an empty name ([#2390](https://github.com/chainguard-dev/apko/pull/2390)). A reproducer has been shared with maintainers separately.

CVE-2026-105768.title: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built ...
CVE-2026-105768.description: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built from apk packages. From version 0.2.0 to before version 1.4.5, UserEntry.Parse and GroupEntry.Parse in pkg/passwd read the UID and GID fields of /etc/passwd and /etc/group entries with strconv.Atoi and convert them to uint32 without a range check. The truncated UID is also used when resolving the image's run-as user. This issue has been fixed in version 1.4.5.

CVE-2026-42575.title: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built ...
CVE-2026-42575.description: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built from apk packages. Prior to version 1.2.7, apko verifies the signature on APKINDEX.tar.gz but never compares individually downloaded .apk packages against the checksum recorded in the signed index. The checksum is parsed and available via ChecksumString(), and the downloaded package control hash is computed, but the two values are never compared in getPackageImpl(). Mismatched packages are silently accepted. An attacker who can substitute download responses (compromised mirror, HTTP repository, poisoned CDN cache) can install arbitrary packages into built images. This issue has been patched in version 1.2.7.

CVE-2026-42576.title: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built ...
CVE-2026-42576.description: apko allows users to build and publish OCI container images built from apk packages. Prior to version 1.2.7, DiscoverKeys in pkg/apk/apk/implementation.go unconditionally type-asserts JWKS keys as *rsa.PublicKey without checking the key type. If a repository JWKS endpoint returns a non-RSA key (e.g. EC), the unchecked assertion panics and crashes apko. This affects any workflow that initializes the APK database and fetches repository keys. This issue has been patched in version 1.2.7.
